_comment: How each place of the catalogue's words-14.jsonl was settled before it went in config/figures-seen/: two readers read every place against its BSB verse, one asking whether the figure is plainly there and one whether the marked words, form and tags are right; a place both passed is kept as handed over, and any place either questioned was read a third time and kept, changed or dropped. A new form stands only where a reader proposed it. Places not read are held, not listed. Stray punctuation before marked words is trimmed, and Strong's tags that light the article (G3588) or the object marker (H0853), or number eight, the search's limit, are taken off as a stretch of words.

Then kept figures of speech were read again by two readers, a third settling any difference ("words re-read" counts them: those a sample showed at risk, such as wide spans, or those found only in the Hebrew or Greek that carry no tags): each kept as it was, cut to the words that carry the figure, or dropped ("words").

Last, a sample of 25 kept places was read by two more readers, a third settling any split; the file goes in only when 24 or more pass, and any place that fails is dropped. "samples" lists each sample and its result.
A place whose verse already has the same form from an earlier file is left out here, since the earlier file's place stands ("same form already on this verse").

places.words_why: The plain is plainly likened to something in "well watered like the garden of the LORD, like the land of Egypt." The marked "like the garden" stops before "of the LORD", and those are the words that say which garden it is like. So the marking should be the whole likeness, "like the garden of the LORD".
"the smoke rising from the land like smoke from a furnace": the likeness is to a furnace, so "like smoke" alone only repeats the word "smoke" and does not show what it is compared to.
"the smoke rose like the smoke of a furnace" is a plain likeness, but "like the smoke" alone leaves out what it is likened to, the furnace.
"face to face, as a man speaks to his friend" is a plain likeness, but "as a man speaks" cuts off "to his friend", which is what the likeness is about.
"make your sky like iron and your land like bronze" holds two plain likenesses in one clause. Marking only "like iron" leaves its pair unlit.

places.why: The verse plainly likens the manna to coriander seed and its look to gum resin, so it is a simile. But the bare verb "resembled" does not carry the likeness. The marked words become the two likenesses as the BSB gives them. There are no Strong's tags to strip.

places.words_why: "Carry them in your bosom, as a nurse carries an infant" is a plain likeness, but "as a nurse carries" cuts off "an infant", which completes it.
"This horde will devour everything around us, as an ox licks up the grass of the field" is a plain likeness, but "as an ox licks" cuts off what the ox licks up, which is the point of the likeness.

places.why: "They spread out like palm groves" is a plain simile, but "like palm" stops in the middle of the likeness. The span is now "like palm groves".
"will not be like sheep without a shepherd" is a plain simile. Its point is "without a shepherd", which is the reason Moses asks for a leader, so the span now covers the whole likeness.
"the LORD your God carried you, as a man carries his son" is a plain simile, but the marked words left out "his son". The span is now the whole likeness.
"chased you like a swarm of bees" is a plain simile, but "like a swarm" leaves out the bees the Amorites are likened to. The span is now "like a swarm of bees".
"just as a man disciplines his son, so the LORD your God disciplines you" is a plain likeness, but the marked words left out "his son". The span is now the whole likeness.

"just like the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim" plainly likens the ruined land to the overthrown cities, but the span stopped after "Sodom", partway through the list. It now covers all four cities.
"came with their livestock and their tents like a great swarm of locusts" is a plain simile, but "like a great swarm" leaves out the locusts. The span is now the whole likeness.
"had settled in the valley like a swarm of locusts" is a plain simile, but "like a swarm" stops before "of locusts". The span is now the whole likeness.

"Men like you ... each one resembling the son of a king" is a literal report of what the men looked like: men compared with men, with no "like" or "as" in the marked words. A careful reader would not take it as a figure.
"he snapped the bowstrings like a strand of yarn seared by a flame" is a plain simile. Its point is yarn that gives way at a touch of fire, so the span now includes "seared by a flame".
"He shall fling away the lives of your enemies like stones from a sling" is a plain simile in the BSB, and the sling is its image. The span is now "like stones from a sling", not just "like stones".

"As a man falls before the wicked, so also you fell" is a plain as/so likeness in David's lament. The marked words stop at "so", which is the start of line 4. The likeness itself is the BSB's line 3, "As a man falls before the wicked".

"bring all the people back to you as a bride returning to her husband" is a plain likeness in the BSB. The marked words cut the image off before "to her husband", so the whole likeness is marked instead.
"The king made silver as common in Jerusalem as stones" is a plain as...as likeness. The marked words end on "as" and leave out "stones", the thing silver is likened to.
"the LORD will strike Israel as a reed is shaken in the water" is a plain likeness. The marked "as a reed is" breaks off before "shaken in the water", the point of the image.

"his flesh was restored and became like that of a little child" compares flesh with flesh. It literally describes his healed skin rather than likening it to something of another kind. Whether it is a figure at all is open to doubt, so it does not go live.
"he had a great army, like the army of God" plainly likens David's army to God's host. The marked "like the army" drops "of God", and without those words nothing is likened to anything.
"The king made silver and gold as common in Jerusalem as stones" is a plain as...as likeness. The marked words end on "as" and leave out "stones", the thing silver and gold are likened to.
"The king made silver as common in Jerusalem as stones" plainly likens silver to stones. The marked words stopped before "stones", the thing it is likened to, so the full likeness is marked.
In an inventory of temple articles, "bronze, as precious as gold" states what the bronze was worth. It is a literal comparison of value between two metals, not a figure.

"You speak as a foolish woman speaks" compares one woman's speech with the speech of foolish women, things of one kind. It reads as a plain rebuke, not a figurative likeness, and when in doubt the place does not go live.
"man is born to trouble as surely as sparks fly upward" is a plain likeness, but the picture is the sparks flying upward. The marked words cut it off, so the whole poetry line is marked.
Forgotten misery is plainly likened to water that has flowed past. The likeness is carried by "as waters gone by". "recalling it only" is the clause around it, so it comes off.

"So man wastes away like something rotten, like a moth-eaten garment" holds two plain likenesses. The marked words ended inside "moth-eaten", which made the likeness a moth and not the garment, so each likeness is marked whole.
"as water wears away the stones ... so You destroy a man's hope" is a plain likeness. "as water wears" cut the verb "wears away" in two, so the whole phrase is marked.
"overwhelming him like a king poised to attack" plainly likens distress to an attacking king. "like a king poised" stopped before "to attack", which the picture needs.

"Is not God as high as the heavens? Look at the highest stars, how lofty they are!" measures God's height, and the next verses place Him there ("He walks on the vault of heaven"). It does not liken God to something unlike Him, so it is a statement of degree, not a plain simile. When in doubt, drop.

places.words_why: "I will come forth as gold" plainly likens tested Job to refined gold, but "come forth" is Job's own action and not part of the likeness. Keep "as gold".

places.why: "As drought and heat consume the melting snow, so Sheol steals those who have sinned" is a plain as/so likeness. The marked words ended on a stray "so", so the words are now the likeness itself.
"The house he built is like a moth’s cocoon" is a plain simile. The marked "like a moth" cut the phrase and likened the house to a moth, so the words are now "like a moth’s cocoon".

The BSB has no "like" or "as", so there is no simile in its words, and the Hebrew "like a robe" in line 2 has no Strong's tags. Line 1, "I put on righteousness, and it clothed me", is a plain metaphor in both the BSB and the Hebrew, with righteousness spoken of as a garment, so it stays as a metaphor at that line.

places.words_why: "multiply my days as the sand" is a plain likeness, but "my days" is what is compared, not the likeness. The figure is carried by "as the sand".

places.why: "drank in my words like spring showers" is a plain simile. The marked "like spring" stopped before the thing compared, so the words are now "like spring showers".
"I have become like dust and ashes" is a plain simile. The likeness is the pair, so the words are now "like dust and ashes".
"his flesh is refreshed like a child’s" likens his flesh to a child's flesh. The marked "like a child" dropped the possessive, so the words are now "like a child’s".
The simile is "drinks up derision like water". "What man is like Job" is a question about people, not a likeness, so it is left out of the words.
places.words_why: "who drinks up derision like water?" is a plain simile, but the marking takes in the verb and its object. "like water" is enough to show the likeness.

places.why: "reflect the heat like a mirror of bronze" plainly likens the skies to a bronze mirror. The words now take the whole likeness, "like a mirror of bronze".
"Now brace yourself like a man" tells Job, who is a man, to act like one. It reads as a set way of saying "bravely", not as one thing plainly likened to another, so the simile is not plain.
"The earth takes shape like clay under a seal" is a plain simile. The image is clay pressed by a seal, so the words are now "like clay under a seal".
This is the same as Job 38:3. "Now brace yourself like a man" tells Job, a man, to act manfully. It is a set way of speaking, not a plain likening of one thing to another.
"He feeds on grass like an ox" compares one grazing beast with another to say plainly what Behemoth eats. It is a literal comparison, and the verse does not show it as a figure. When in doubt, drop.

The BSB has no "like" or "as", and the Hebrew "like rods of iron" in line 2 has no Strong's tags, so there is no simile to show. Line 1, "His bones are tubes of bronze", says the bones are the thing they are like in both the BSB and the Hebrew, so it is a plain metaphor at that line.
places.words_why: "His bones are tubes of bronze" is a plain metaphor, since bones are not bronze. The words used for something else are "tubes of bronze", so marking fewer words is enough.

places.why: "A club is regarded as straw" plainly likens the club to straw. The marked words took the whole verse, but "and he laughs at the sound of the lance" has no likeness in it, so the span is cut to the first line.
places.words_why: "A club is regarded as straw" plainly likens a club to straw, as "like chaff" does in the verse before. The marking takes in the whole line, and "as straw" carries the likeness.

places.why: "he makes the sea like a jar of ointment" is a plain likeness. "like a jar" cut off what the sea is likened to, so the span becomes "like a jar of ointment".
same form already on this verse (psalm-14-4-simile-seen)

The BSB reads "You will place them in a fiery furnace", with no "like" or "as" and no likeness. The search's note shows the likeness is only in the Hebrew (ke-tannur), and the place has no Strong's tags on those words, so it cannot go live.
"Do not be like the horse or mule" is a plain likeness. It names both animals, so the span becomes "like the horse or mule".
"You have given us up as sheep to be devoured" is a plain likeness. The marked words ended on a dangling "to be", so the span becomes "as sheep to be devoured".
"we are considered as sheep to be slaughtered" is a plain likeness. The marked words ended on a dangling "to be", so the span becomes "as sheep to be slaughtered".
same form already on this verse (psalm-53-4-simile-seen)

"As smoke is blown away, You will drive them out; as wax melts before the fire, the wicked will perish" holds two plain likenesses. The mark "As smoke is" stops mid-clause, so it now marks both likenesses in full.

"May its fruit trees flourish like the forests of Lebanon, and its people like the grass of the field" holds two plain likenesses. The mark "like the forests" cuts the phrase, so it now marks both likenesses in full.
same form already on this verse (psalm-73-20-simile-seen)
The foes wrecking the sanctuary (74:4, 74:6) are plainly likened to woodcutters. The whole one-line verse carries the likeness, so "of trees" is added.

"twisted like a faulty bow" is a plain simile. "faithless like their fathers" is a literal comparison with real people, not a figure, and the old mark ran across both lines. Only line 2 is now marked.
places.words_why: The likeness "like a faulty bow" is plain in "twisted like a faulty bow." The verb "twisted" sits beside it and does not carry the figure, so it is cut.

places.why: "As fire consumes a forest, as a flame sets the mountains ablaze, so pursue them with Your tempest" (83:14-15) is a plain as/so likeness. "As fire consumes" drops the object, so it now marks both lines of the likeness in full.

The BSB has no "like" or "as": "a thousand years are but a day that passes". The likeness shows only in the Hebrew ke-, and the place has no Strong's tags on that word, so it cannot go live as a simile. Calling it a metaphor would mislabel what the Hebrew plainly says, so when in doubt it does not go live.
"The righteous will flourish like a palm tree" is a plain likeness with "like", but the marked "like a palm" cuts the likeness short. The words should be "like a palm tree".
"I am like a desert owl" is a plain likeness. The marked "like a desert" leaves out the bird he is likened to, so the words should be "like a desert owl".
"your youth is renewed like the eagle’s" is a plain likeness. The marked "like the eagle" stops inside the BSB's word "eagle’s", so the words should be the whole word as the BSB spells it.

"He wraps Himself in light as with a garment" plainly likens the light to a garment. The marked span starts in the middle of "in light" and takes in the thing likened. The words that carry the likeness are "as with a garment", which matches how the other similes are marked.
same form already on this verse (psalm-118-12-simile-seen)
same form already on this verse (psalm-125-2-simile-seen)
"the night shines like the day" is a plain likeness. The marked words ran past the line break into "for darkness", so they are cut back to the likeness itself.
same form already on this verse (psalm-141-7-simile-seen)

"Like a gold ring in a pig's snout is a beautiful woman who lacks discretion" is a plain likeness. The marked words "Like a gold" stopped partway through the image, so they now cover the whole of it, which is the BSB's line 1.
"his favor is like a rain cloud in spring" is a plain likeness. The marked words "like a rain" left out "cloud", the thing compared, so they now cover the whole likeness.
same form already on this verse (proverbs-25-3-simile-seen)
A plain simile. The likeness turns on "without rain", which "Like clouds" leaves out, so the words are now the whole image.

places.words_why: "Like a club or sword or sharp arrow is a man who bears false witness" is a plain simile. The likeness is the whole list in line 1, and the mark stops partway, leaving "or sharp arrow" unlit.
"Like a broken tooth or a foot out of joint is confidence in a faithless man" likens the confidence to both things. The mark lights only the first, so the likeness should take in all of line 1.

places.why: A plain simile with two images under one "Like". "on a cold day" is the point of the first image and the second image is governed by the same "Like", so the words now cover both images.
same form already on this verse (proverbs-25-23-simile-seen)

places.words_why: "Like a muddied spring or a polluted well is a righteous man who gives way to the wicked" is a plain simile with two pictures. The mark leaves out "or a polluted well", which is part of the same likeness.

places.why: A plain simile. "Like a city whose walls" breaks off before "are broken down", which is the point, so the words are now the whole image.
A plain simile: things out of season. "Like snow" alone loses "in summer", which is the point, so the words are now the whole image line.

places.words_why: "Like a fluttering sparrow or darting swallow, an undeserved curse does not come to rest" names both birds in the likeness. The mark lights only the sparrow.
"Like cutting off one’s own feet or drinking violence is the sending of a message by the hand of a fool" gives a two-part likeness. The mark leaves out "or drinking violence".

places.why: A plain simile. The image is a stone bound "into a sling", and the marked words cut that off, so the words are now the whole image line.
A plain simile. The image is a thorn in a drunkard's hand, and "Like a thorn" alone misses that, so the words are now the whole image line.
A plain simile. The point is "who wounds at random", which "Like an archer" leaves out, so the words are now the whole image line.
same form already on this verse (proverbs-26-11-simile-seen)
same form already on this verse (proverbs-26-14-simile-seen)

places.words_why: "Like one who grabs a dog by the ears is a passerby who meddles in a quarrel not his own" is a plain simile. The picture is grabbing the dog "by the ears", and the mark cuts that off mid-phrase.

"Like a madman shooting firebrands and deadly arrows, so is the man who deceives his neighbor" (26:18-19) is a plain simile. The madman shoots both firebrands "and deadly arrows", so the likeness runs through the whole of 26:18.

places.why: same form already on this verse (proverbs-26-21-simile-seen)
A plain simile. The likeness is the bird straying from its nest, which "Like a bird" alone misses, so the words are now the whole image line.
same form already on this verse (proverbs-27-17-simile-seen)
same form already on this verse (proverbs-27-19-simile-seen)
A plain as...so likeness: the stirring of anger brings strife as churning milk yields butter. The opening "For" is not part of the figure, so it is dropped.
places.words_why: "For as the churning of milk yields butter, and the twisting of the nose draws blood, so the stirring of anger brings forth strife" is a plain comparison, but the marked words end on a loose "so" that belongs to the other half of the comparison.

places.why: "wisdom exceeds folly, just as light exceeds darkness" is a plain comparison. The marked "as light exceeds" stopped before its object, so the span is now the whole likeness.

The BSB's "As a dream comes through many cares, so the speech of a fool..." is a plain as/so likeness. "As a dream comes" left out the point of the comparison, so the span is now the whole first line.
"as many dreams bring futility, so do many words" sets words beside dreams in a plain as/so likeness. The opening "For" is not part of the figure, so it is dropped.
places.words_why: "For as many dreams bring futility, so do many words" is a plain comparison, but the marked words end on a loose "so" that opens the other half.

places.why: "Exactly as a man is born, so he will depart" says he leaves in the same state he came (see 5:15). That is a match of manner, not one thing likened to another, and the marked "as a man is" is a broken fragment.
"wisdom, like money, is a shelter" likens wisdom to money. The likeness is "like money". "is a shelter" is what is said of wisdom and does not belong in the span.
"I am dark, yet lovely ... like the tents of Kedar, like the curtains of Solomon" holds two plain likenesses that fill line 2. "like the tents" cut the first one off before "of Kedar".
"Why should I be like a veiled woman" is a plain likeness. The marked span ran into the next line and stopped at "flocks", so it is now just the likeness.

"I compare you, my darling, to a mare among Pharaoh’s chariots" states the likeness outright. "I compare you" left out what she is compared to, so the image is added and the address "my darling" is left out.
"Your teeth are like a flock of newly shorn sheep" is a plain simile. "like a flock" cut the image off before what kind of flock it is.
"Your lips are like a scarlet ribbon" and "Your brow ... is like a slice of pomegranate" are plain similes. "like a scarlet" broke off before its noun.
"Your neck is like the tower of David" is a plain simile. "like the tower" left out which tower is meant.
"His cheeks are like beds of spice, towers of perfume" and "His lips are like lilies" are plain similes. The marked span stopped at a stray "towers", so it now runs to the end of the phrase.
places.words_why: "His cheeks are like beds of spice" and "His lips are like lilies" are plain likenesses with "like". "towers of perfume" is a second picture on its own line with no "like" of its own, so mark fewer: only the likenesses with their "like".

places.why: "Your hair is like a flock of goats" is a plain simile. "like a flock" left out "of goats".
"Your teeth are like a flock of sheep" is a plain simile. "like a flock" left out "of sheep".
"Your stature is like a palm tree" is a plain simile, but the marked "like a palm" cuts the BSB's "palm tree" in half; the likeness is "like a palm tree".

places.words_why: "May your breasts be like clusters of the vine" is a plain likeness, but the marked "like clusters" cuts the phrase in half and leaves out what the clusters are. The likeness is "like clusters of the vine".

places.why: The BSB "draw iniquity with cords of deceit and pull sin along with cart ropes" has no "like" or "as". The simile is only in a Hebrew prefix that carries no Strong's tags, and the whole verse is marked. In English it is at most an implied picture, so it is not plain enough to go live unsigned.

"as a tongue of fire consumes the straw, and as dry grass shrivels in the flame, so their roots will decay" is a plain comparison. The marked words take in "Therefore," and end on a stray "so"; the likeness is the two "as" lines.
same form already on this verse (isaiah-6-13-simile-seen)

"the lion will eat straw like the ox" is an ordinary comparison of what two animals eat: the lion will really eat straw as the ox does. Nothing is likened to an unlike thing, so it is not plainly a figure. When in doubt, drop.

"the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the sea is full of water" is a plain simile, but "as the sea is" breaks off before the likeness. The span is the BSB line "as the sea is full of water".

"a tumult on the mountains, like that of a great multitude" describes the noise of what really is a multitude, since the verse ends "The LORD of Hosts is mobilizing an army for war" and 13:5 says "They are coming from faraway lands". The likeness is literal, so a careful reader would not plainly see a figure here. When in doubt, drop.
"will be overthrown by God like Sodom and Gomorrah" is a plain simile, but "like Sodom" cuts off half of the pair. The span is the BSB line "like Sodom and Gomorrah".

"In three years, as a hired worker counts the years" is a plain likeness with "as": the years will be counted as exactly as a hired worker counts his. The marked words drop the object, so the span is "as a hired worker counts the years".
"The nations rage like the rush of many waters" is a plain simile. "like the rush" stopped before the image, so the words are now the whole likeness.

"as a hired worker would count it" tells how the year is reckoned (exactly, the way a hireling counts his term). It compares manner, like "as the LORD commanded". It does not liken one thing to another to illustrate it. The case is doubtful, so the place stays out.
"Moab will be trampled ... as straw is trodden into the dung pile" is a plain simile. The marked words ended on "is", so they are now BSB line 4, the whole likeness.
same form already on this verse (isaiah-26-17-simile-seen)

places.words_why: "For your dew is like the dew of the morning" is a plain likeness. But "like the dew" on its own compares dew with dew and shows nothing. The image is in "of the morning", so the likeness needs it.

places.why: Two as-when likenesses are applied by "So will it be for all the many nations", which makes a plain extended simile. The marks covered the whole verse, including the thing compared, so they are now the two likenesses only (BSB lines 1 to 2 and 3 to 4).

In "You have turned things upside down, as if the potter were regarded as clay", the "as if" clause says what their reversal amounts to. The figure that carries the verse is the potter-and-clay picture of Maker and made, and that likeness is left unsaid. A plain simile is not clearly there, and when in doubt the place is dropped.

"The light of the moon will be as bright as the sun" measures how bright one light will be against another light. It predicts a degree of brightness and does not liken one thing to a different thing to illustrate it. That is not plainly a simile, so the place stays out.

"You will sing as on the night of a holy festival" plainly likens the coming song to singing at a festival. The marked words "as on the night" stop short of what the song is likened to. The likeness is all of line 2, "as on the night of a holy festival".

"The breath of the LORD, like a torrent of burning sulfur, sets it ablaze" is a plain likeness. The breath is likened to a torrent of burning sulfur, not to a torrent alone, so the marked words should be "like a torrent of burning sulfur".

The BSB reads "He turns them to dust with his sword, to windblown chaff with his bow" with no likeness word. The likeness (ke-afar, ke-qash) shows only in the Hebrew, but the place has no Strong's tags and its marked words are the whole verse. The rule says a figure seen only in the Hebrew needs tags on the words that carry it, so the place is dropped.
"the wicked are like the storm-tossed sea" is a plain likeness. The wicked are likened to the sea, so the marked words must not stop at "storm".
"Raise your voice like a ram’s horn" plainly likens the voice to a horn. The marked "like a ram" turns it into a ram, so the span must include "’s horn".
same form already on this verse (isaiah-60-8-simile-seen)
Being wrapped in righteousness "as a bridegroom wears a priestly headdress" is a plain likeness. The marked words stopped before what he wears, so the span is the whole BSB line 5.

places.words_why: "For as the earth brings forth its growth ... so the Lord GOD will cause righteousness ... to spring up" is a plain likeness, but "For" and "so" are not part of the likeness; keep the two "as" clauses.
"For as a young man marries a young woman, so your sons will marry you" is a plain likeness, but the marked words take in "For" and "so"; keep the likeness with its "as".

places.why: same form already on this verse (isaiah-64-2-simile-seen)

"As the new wine is found in a cluster of grapes ... so I will act on behalf of My servants" is a plain as/so likeness. The marked "As the new wine is" broke off mid-clause, so the span is the whole BSB line 2.

places.words_why: "For as is the lifetime of a tree, so will be the days of My people" is a plain likeness, but "For" and "so" are not part of it; keep the "as" clause.

places.why: In "the lion will eat straw like the ox" the "like" compares how two animals really feed: the lion is said to eat straw just as the ox does. That is a plain comparison of fact. It does not liken one thing to something different in kind, so a careful reader would not plainly see a simile here. When in doubt, drop.
"whoever sacrifices a lamb is like one who breaks a dog’s neck" is a plain likeness. The marked words cut off "’s neck", which changes what they say.
same form already on this verse (isaiah-66-13-simile-seen)

"As the thief is ashamed when he is caught, so the house of Israel is disgraced" is a plain as/so likeness. The marked words stopped before "ashamed", the point of the likeness, so the span is the whole BSB line 1.

"as a woman may betray her husband, so you have betrayed Me" is a plain likeness. The marked words start with a stray "But" and end on the joining "so"; the likeness is "as a woman may betray her husband".

"As a well gushes its water, so she pours out her evil" is a plain likeness. The marked words stop before "its water", the thing set against "her evil"; the likeness is the whole first line, "As a well gushes its water".

"the altars ... are as many as the streets of Jerusalem" gives a count (an altar for every street). It does not say one thing is like another, so it is not plainly a simile, and the marked words also cut off "of Jerusalem".
"Is not My inheritance to Me like a speckled bird of prey" is a plain likeness. The marked words split "bird of prey"; the likeness is the whole poetry line, "like a speckled bird of prey".

"just as a loincloth clings to a man's waist, so I have made the whole house of Israel ... cling to Me" is a plain likeness. The marked words add a stray "For" and the joining "so"; the likeness is "just as a loincloth clings to a man’s waist".
"like a warrior powerless to save" is a plain likeness, but "like a warrior" alone loses the point of it, which is in "powerless to save". The words should be the whole poetry line.

"Like a partridge hatching eggs it did not lay is the man who makes a fortune unjustly" is a plain likeness. The point of it is in "hatching eggs it did not lay", so the words should be the whole first poetry line.
"can I not treat you as this potter treats his clay?" is a plain likeness. The marked words stop before "his clay", the thing set against Israel; the likeness is "as this potter treats his clay".

The BSB reads "His message becomes a fire burning in my heart, shut up in my bones", with no "like" or "as", so the figure a BSB reader plainly sees is a metaphor: God's word is called a fire. The "like" is only in the Hebrew, and this place has no Strong's tags. It stays under metaphor with the same words.

"I will make this house like Shiloh" compares one sanctuary's fate with another's: the temple will be ruined as Shiloh was (compare 7:12-14). It is a literal historical comparison of like with like, not a figurative likeness, so the figure is in doubt and the place does not go live.

"this house will become like Shiloh" is the crowd repeating the literal comparison of fate from 26:6. It is a historical example of the same kind of thing, not a figurative likeness, so it does not go live.
"keep them as a shepherd keeps his flock" plainly likens the LORD to a shepherd. The marked words stopped at "keeps" and left out "his flock". The likeness is the BSB's whole line 4.

places.words_why: "As the hosts of heaven cannot be counted and as the sand on the seashore cannot be measured, so too will I multiply the descendants" is a plain likeness. But the marking runs on to a stray "so", so it is cut to the two "as" likenesses.

places.why: "he will wrap himself with the land of Egypt as a shepherd wraps himself in his garment" is a plain simile. The marked words stopped at "wraps" and left out the garment, which is the point of the likeness.
"He has laid waste His tabernacle like a garden booth" is a plain simile. The likeness is the booth, so the marked words must take in "booth" and not stop at "garden".
"as they faint like the wounded" is a plain simile. "in the streets of the city" is the next poetry line and says where they faint, as in 2:11; it is not part of the likeness.

"I compare you" belongs to the question "To what can I compare you". The question asks for a likeness and gives none, so there is no simile at the marked words. The verse's real simile, "as deep as the sea", is a different span from what this search found.

Sons once worth their weight in gold "are now esteemed as jars of clay": a plain simile. The marked words take in the verb and cut off "of clay", which is where the point lies, so they should be "as jars of clay".

The BSB has no likeness word here: 'was the appearance of glowing coals of fire, or of torches' describes what the vision showed. The Hebrew ke- in the note has no Strong's tags, and the marked words are the whole verse.

'the likeness of a throne of sapphire' is how the vision is described, not a plain likeness with 'like' or 'as' in the BSB. The Hebrew in the note has no tags, and the marked words are the whole verse.
'the wheels gleamed like a beryl stone' plainly likens the wheels' gleam to beryl. The marked words stop before 'stone', so they become 'like a beryl stone'.
'all four had the same form, like a wheel within a wheel' describes how the wheels were built. It does not liken them to something of another kind, so the figure is not plain.

'As silver is melted in a furnace, so you will be melted within the city' is a plain likeness. The marked words break off at 'As silver is', so they become the whole likeness, 'As silver is melted in a furnace'.

'they slept with her as with a prostitute' says how they treated her. Verse 43 says 'for that is all she is', so the 'as' names her role rather than likening her to something else. It is doubtful as a simile.
'I will raise up many nations against you, as the sea brings up its waves' plainly likens the nations to waves. The marked words cut off at 'brings', so they become 'as the sea brings up its waves'.

'as an army entering a breached city' likens an army breaking into a city to an army entering a breached city. That is close to a plain description of what happens, so it is doubtful as a figure. The marked words are also the whole verse.
'Pharaoh, who will groan before him like a mortally wounded man' is a plain likeness. The marked words leave out 'man', so they become 'like a mortally wounded man'.
'This land that was desolate has become like the garden of Eden' is a plain likeness. The marked words leave out 'of Eden', which names the garden, so they become 'like the garden of Eden'.
The princes of the earth are plainly likened to sacrificial animals at God's feast. The marked words stopped at "rams" and cut off the rest of the list, so the span now covers the whole likeness.

"a structure that resembled a city" just says what the buildings in the vision looked like. That is plain description, not a figure. The lone word "resembled" also leaves out what the structure is likened to.
"fish of many kinds, like the fish of the Great Sea" compares fish with fish to say how many kinds there will be. That is a plain statement, not a likeness drawn for force.

"as the toes ... were partly iron and partly clay, so this kingdom will be partly strong and partly brittle" explains what part of the dream stands for. It is not a likeness. The span also starts on "And" and ends on "so".

"One like the Son of Man" describes how the One in the vision looked, and the BSB sets "the Son of Man" as a title. Calling it a figure of likeness is not plain and could mislead, so when in doubt it stays out.

"As surely as the sun rises, He will appear" plainly likens how sure His coming is to the sunrise. The marked "as the sun rises" dropped "surely" and reads like a time clause, so the span is now the whole poetry line.
"your loyalty is like a morning mist" plainly likens their loyalty to mist that does not last. The marked "like a morning" cut off the image itself, so the span now ends at "mist".

"their sacrifices ... will be to them like the bread of mourners; all who eat will be defiled" is a plain likeness with "like". The point is the bread of mourners, which defiles, so the span must hold the whole image, not stop at "like the bread".

"How could I make you like Admah? How could I treat you like Zeboiim?" sets one people's fate beside another people's fate. That is a literal comparison of like with like, not one thing likened to a thing of another kind. Seeing what "like Admah" means also needs Admah's history, which the verse does not give. When in doubt, drop.
"they will be like the morning mist" is a plain simile. They are likened to the mist, so the span must end on "mist", not on "like the morning".
"The land before them is like the Garden of Eden" is a plain simile. "like the Garden" cuts the name in half, so the span must be the whole name.

"As the shepherd snatches from the mouth of the lion two legs or a piece of an ear, so the Israelites ... will be rescued" is a plain as/so simile. The likeness runs across poetry lines 2 and 3, and the span must include what is snatched, not stop at "snatches".

"I will make you like My signet ring" is a plain likeness with "like". The marked words stopped at "signet" and cut the noun in two, so the words become "like My signet ring".
"woke me, as a man is awakened from his sleep" is a plain likeness with "as". The marked words stopped before the verb that makes the comparison, so they become "as a man is awakened from his sleep".
"refine them like gold and silver" is a plain simile; the likeness is "like gold and silver", which "like gold" cut in half.
"I will spare them as a man spares his own son who serves him" is a plain simile; the marked words stopped before the son, who makes the likeness.
"is like a foolish man who built his house on sand" is a plain simile; the marked words ended on a dangling "who".

"as Jonah was ... so the Son of Man will be" is a plain as/so likeness. A type could also be read here, but the simile is the one that plainly shows in the words. The span loses the opening "For" and the dangling "so".
"The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed good seed" is a plain likeness; the marked words left out what it is like.
"The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed" is a plain likeness; the marked words stopped before the mustard seed.
"The kingdom of heaven is like leaven" is a plain likeness; the marked words left out the leaven.
"As the weeds are collected and burned in the fire, so will it be at the end of the age" is a plain as/so likeness; "As the weeds are" cut off in the middle of the clause.
"The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field" is a plain likeness; the marked words left out the treasure.
"the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant in search of fine pearls" is a plain likeness; the marked words left out the merchant.
"the kingdom of heaven is like a net that was cast into the sea" is a plain likeness; the marked words left out the net.
"every scribe ... is like a homeowner who brings out of his storeroom new treasures as well as old" is a plain simile; the marked words were the subject, not the likeness.

The BSB says "faith the size of a mustard seed", with no "like" or "as". The likeness rests only on the Greek "hos", and the place has no Strong's tags on it, so a BSB reader does not plainly see a simile.
"the kingdom of heaven is like a king who wanted to settle accounts" is a plain likeness; the marked words left out the king.
"the kingdom of heaven is like a landowner who went out early" is a plain likeness; the marked words left out the landowner.
"The kingdom of heaven is like a king who prepared a wedding banquet" is a plain likeness; the marked words left out the king.
"the kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins who took their lamps" is a plain likeness; the marked words left out the ten virgins.
places.words_why: "the kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins" is a plain likeness, but the rest ("who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom") is the story, not the likeness itself.

places.why: "He will separate the people ... as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats" is a plain simile; "as a shepherd separates" stopped before the sheep and goats that make the likeness.

"to arrest Me as you would an outlaw?" says how they are really treating Him. It is a plain statement of manner, not a likeness between two unlike things. The figure in the verse is the question, so a reader is not plainly shown a simile, and when in doubt the place drops.

"The kingdom of God is like a man who scatters seed on the ground" is a plain likeness. The marked "kingdom of God is like" leaves out the picture it is likened to, so the words become the likeness itself.

"as Jonah was a sign to the Ninevites, so the Son of Man will be a sign" plainly uses Jonah's case as the picture of what is coming. The marked words open with a stray "For" and end on a dangling "so", so they are cut down to the likeness clause.
The BSB reads "faith the size of a mustard seed", with no "like" or "as". The likeness word is only in the Greek, and no Strong's tags point at it, so the figure is not plain in the words shown.

Lightning lighting the sky from end to end is a plain picture of how the Son of Man will come in His day. The marked words open with a stray "For" and end on a dangling "so", so they are cut down to the picture.

"Just as it was in the days of Noah, so also will it be in the days of the Son of Man" plainly likens the coming days to Noah's days, and 17:27 fills in the picture. The marked words end on a dangling "so", so they are cut down to the likeness clause.

"just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life" says the Son truly does the same work as the Father. Nothing is pictured by something of another kind, so it is a plain statement, not plainly a figure. Calling it a simile could also suggest it is not meant literally.

"Just as the living Father sent Me and I live because of the Father, so also the one who feeds on Me will live because of Me" sets two real relationships side by side. There is no image from another kind of thing, so it is not plainly a simile, and when in doubt the place stays out.

The branch that bears fruit only in the vine is a plain picture of the disciples, who bear fruit only by remaining in Christ. The marked "as no branch can" splits off "Just" and cuts the picture short, so the words become the whole likeness clause.

"As the Father has sent Me, so also I am sending you" sets one real sending beside another, as a pattern. It does not liken anything to a thing of a different kind, so it is not a plain simile. The marked words also stop at "so".
"we are considered as sheep to be slaughtered" is a plain likeness. The marked words broke off before "slaughtered" and now take in the whole likeness.

"As was the earthly man, so also are those who are of the earth" states a plain correspondence of nature. It is not a likeness drawn from a different thing. The marked words also stop at "so".

"just as the sufferings of Christ overflow to us, so also ... our comfort overflows" is a literal proportion: as much suffering, so much comfort. It is not a simile, and the marked words break off at "so".
"as the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit" is a command with a pattern to follow, not a figurative likeness. The marked words also end at "so".

places.words_why: "in which you shine as lights in the world" is a plain likeness, but the verb "shine" beside it does not carry the figure; the likeness is "as lights".

places.why: "we treated each of you as a father treats his own children" is a plain likeness. The marked words stopped at the verb and now include its object.

"being chained like a criminal" says how Paul is literally treated, really in chains as criminals are; it is a plain comparison of treatment, not a figure a reader would clearly see. When in doubt, drop.

"passed through the Red Sea as on dry land" tells how they really crossed: the sea bed was dry ground (Exodus 14:22). The "as" gives the manner of the crossing, not a likeness between two different things. Since a reader may well take it literally, it is not a plain simile, and in doubt it is dropped.
"is like a man who looks at his face in a mirror" is a plain likeness. The marked words broke off at "looks" and now run through "in a mirror".
